t.6.27.1: But the ten-faced Daśānana, evil-minded and fallen under the sway of Time, could not bear those beneficial words spoken by Mālyavant.
t.6.27.2: Knitting a frown upon his face, he came under the sway of anger, and with eyes rolling in indignation he then spoke to Mālyavant.
t.6.27.3: Such harsh and harmful words, spoken as if with good intent by one who has gone over to the enemy's side, have never reached my ears.
t.6.27.4: By what reasoning do you consider Rāma capable, a mere wretched man, alone, relying on monkeys for support, abandoned by his father and dwelling in the forest?
t.6.27.5: Me, the lord of the Rākṣasas, who strike terror into the gods, me who am lacking in no form of valor, by what reasoning do you consider me inferior?
t.6.27.6: I suspect that you have spoken these harsh words to me either out of hatred for heroes, or out of partiality for the enemy, or at the instigation of others.
t.6.27.7: For what learned man, knowing the true meaning of the śāstras, would speak harsh words to a mighty one firmly established in his position, unless he were urged on by the enemy?
t.6.27.8: Having brought Sītā from the forest, like Śrī bereft of her lotus, why should I give her back out of fear of Rāghava?
t.6.27.9: Within a few days you shall see Rāghava, surrounded by crores of monkeys, together with Sugrīva and with Lakṣmaṇa, slain by me.
t.6.27.10: Even the gods cannot stand against him in single combat on the battlefield; why then would that Rāvaṇa take on fear in war?
t.6.27.11: I might even be broken in two, yet I would never bow to anyone. This is an inborn flaw of mine, a nature that is hard to overcome.
t.6.27.12: If indeed a bridge has been built across the ocean by Rāma through mere chance, what marvel is there in this, by which fear has come upon you?
t.6.27.13: But that Rāma, having crossed the ocean together with the army of monkeys, will not return alive; this I truly promise you.
t.6.27.14: Perceiving that Rāvaṇa, speaking thus, was agitated and enraged, Mālyavān, abashed, offered no word in reply.
t.6.27.15: Having duly honored the king with blessings for his victory, as was fitting, Mālyavān, granted leave, went to his own dwelling.
t.6.27.16: But Rāvaṇa, the Rākṣasa, together with his ministers, having taken counsel and deliberated, caused an unequalled defence to be arranged in Laṅkā.
t.6.27.17: And he assigned the rākṣasa Prahasta to the eastern gate, and to the southern gate the two mighty ones, Mahāpārśva and Mahodara.
t.6.27.18: Then, likewise, at the western gate he stationed his son Indrajit, master of great magic, surrounded by many rākṣasas.
t.6.27.19: Having posted Śuka and Sāraṇa at the northern gate of the city, he said to those ministers, "And I myself will be here too."
t.6.27.20: And he stationed the rākṣasa Virūpākṣa, of great valour and prowess, in the central troop, together with many rākṣasas.
t.6.27.21: Having made such arrangements in Laṅkā, the bull among rākṣasas, fallen into the power of Death, considered himself to have achieved his purpose.
t.6.27.22: Then, having ordered ample arrangements for the city, he dismissed his ministers; and, honored by the assembly of counselors with blessings for victory, he entered his great and opulent inner palace.
